title: Ike in the mud
pull: The boss comes to the front

facts.text: On 10 November 1944, Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Supreme Allied Commander, went to the front lines of the U.S. Ninth Army on the German and Dutch border.
At Herzogenrath, Germany, he climbed out of his jeep, pulled off his raincoat, and was greeted by Maj. Gen. Leland Hobbs of the 30th Infantry Division.
Riding with him were Lt. Gen. Omar Bradley, Lt. Gen. William H. Simpson of the Ninth Army, and Maj. Gen. Raymond McLain of XIX Corps.
Near Eigelshoven in the Netherlands, he walked a muddy wood to talk with men of the 29th Infantry Division, commanded by Maj. Gen. Charles Gerhardt.
An Army photographer caught him standing in the fallen leaves, hands on hips, speaking to soldiers of the 2nd Battalion, 175th Infantry, in their raincoats and helmets.
These were the men about to make Operation Queen, the big push toward the Roer River. Bad weather had already pushed its start back from 5 November and then from 10 November.
Queen finally opened on 16 November with one of the heaviest air attacks of the war in support of ground troops: 1,204 American heavy bombers dropped 4,120 bombs ahead of the First and Ninth Armies.
The 29th and 30th Infantry Divisions and the 2nd Armored Division led the Ninth Army's part of the attack.
The Americans reached the Roer in about a month of hard fighting but could not cross it before the Germans struck in the Ardennes on 16 December.
The Ninth Army alone lost 1,133 killed, 6,864 wounded, and 2,059 missing in the offensive.
Army Signal Corps film of the visit shows his jeep arriving, Eisenhower greeting the generals, and Eisenhower walking among the troops in the wet woods.

photoNote: Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower talks to men of the 2nd Battalion, 175th Infantry, 29th Infantry Division at the front, 10 November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo 111-SC-196364 (photographer Moore), NARA, public domain. Taken on the day. The NARA title says 375th but the print caption reads 175th, which is the 29th Division regiment. Downloaded from NARA at full size (3231 px) and saved at 2400 px.

declassified.fact: The Americans were not bombing alone when Queen began. The same day, 467 RAF heavy bombers struck the German towns of Duren and Julich, and 180 more hit Heinsberg, part of a plan that called for more than 4,500 Allied aircraft.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Army Signal Corps film, stories LIB 511 (Herzogenrath, Germany) and LIB 512 (Eigelshoven, Netherlands), both dated 10 Nov 1944 on the shot card, with a slate in the film reading 10 Nov 1944. Silent. The file is the stretch from 3:10 to 7:10 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times (checked on a contact sheet of the file): 0:00 to 0:06 a truck, then the LIB 511 title card at about 0:08; 0:14 to 0:45 Eisenhower climbs out of his jeep, pulls off his raincoat, and greets Hobbs, with Simpson and Bradley, the best opener (start at about 0:15 on the movement); 0:48 to 1:00 generals at the jeeps; 1:02 to 1:15 the cameraman's slate reading General Eisenhower, 30th Inf Div, Herzogenrath, 10 Nov 1944; 1:18 to 1:50 jeeps pull up at headquarters; 2:00 LIB 512 title card; 2:10 to 3:45 Eisenhower walks a muddy wood and talks with 29th Division troops, with close shots of his face at about 3:18 to 3:36. The reel's first three minutes (St Lo trains, 7 Nov) are left out.

body:
Six days before 1,204 American heavy bombers opened the way, the Supreme Allied Commander stood in the mud with the men who would go in first.

10 November 1944. Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower went to the front lines of the U.S. Ninth Army on the German and Dutch border. At Herzogenrath he climbed out of his jeep, pulled off his raincoat, and was greeted by Maj. Gen. Leland Hobbs of the 30th Infantry Division. Lt. Gen. Omar Bradley rode with him.

Near Eigelshoven in the Netherlands, he walked a muddy wood to talk with men of the 29th Infantry Division. An Army photographer caught him in the fallen leaves, hands on hips, speaking to soldiers of the 175th Infantry in their raincoats and helmets.

These were the men about to make Operation Queen, the push toward the Roer River, already put off twice by bad weather. It opened on 16 November behind one of the heaviest air attacks of the war in support of ground troops.

The Americans reached the Roer in about a month of hard fighting. The Ninth Army alone lost 1,133 killed.
